claim: Obesity and physical inactivity are major risk factors for type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular diseases and several types of cancer.
source: Obesity and physical inactivity are major risk factors for a number of chronic diseases, such as type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular diseases and several types of cancer.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about risk factors for chronic diseases.

claim: The epidemic of obesity and sedentary lifestyle is a major burden on public health systems worldwide.
source: Today's epidemic of obesity and sedentary lifestyle is thus a major burden on public health systems worldwide (GBD 2019 Risk Factors Collaborators, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to GBD 2019 Risk Factors Collaborators, 2020.

claim: Physical inactivity and increased sedentary time are associated with a higher risk of obesity according to observational studies.
source: Many observational studies suggest that physical inactivity and increased sedentary time are associated with a higher risk of obesity (Lee et al., 2010; Du et al., 2013; Silva et al., 2019; Myers et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to observational studies.

claim: Some studies have indicated a reverse effect where obesity leads to physical inactivity and increased sedentary time.
source: However, other studies have indicated a reverse effect, where obesity leads to physical inactivity and increased sedentary time (Petersen et al., 2004; Mortensen et al., 2006; Bak et al., 2004; Barone Gibbs et al., 2020; Ekelund et al., 2008; Myers et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to studies showing reverse causality.

claim: Randomized clinical trials of physical activity interventions have indicated that the causal effects of physical activity on body weight are modest.
source: Furthermore, randomized clinical trials of physical activity interventions have indicated that the causal effects of physical activity on body weight are modest (Church et al., 2009; Rosenkilde et al., 2012; Golubic et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to randomized clinical trials.

claim: The strong inverse relationship between physical activity and body weight observed in cross-sectional epidemiological studies may be affected by bias such as reverse causality or confounding.
source: This suggests that the observational results may be affected by bias, such as reverse causality or confounding by other lifestyle or environmental factors (Schnurr et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing observational studies with RCT results, supported by citation.

claim: The causal relationships between physical inactivity, sedentary time and adiposity remain unclear.
source: To date, the causal relationships between physical inactivity, sedentary time and adiposity remain unclear and warrant further investigation.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the conflicting evidence presented in the introduction.

claim: It is important to assess the causal relationship with adiposity separately for physical activity and sedentary time because individuals can be physically active even if they spend substantial time in sedentary behaviors.
source: It is important to assess the causal relationship with adiposity separately for physical activity and sedentary time, as individuals can be physically active even if they engaged a substantial part of their time to sedentary behaviors, and vice versa (Panahi and Tremblay, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation and represents established knowledge about the independence of physical activity and sedentary behavior.

claim: Mendelian randomization is a powerful method to minimize the influence of reverse causality and confounding on causal estimates derived from observational data.
source: Mendelian randomization is a powerful method to minimize the influence of reverse causality and confounding on causal estimates derived from observational data.
evidence: This is established methodological knowledge about Mendelian randomization.

claim: Genotypes are randomly allocated at conception.
source: Since genotypes are randomly allocated at conception, genetic alleles associated with physical activity, sedentary behavior, and body mass index (BMI) can be used to assign individuals according to higher or lower mean levels of these exposures in a randomized manner (Figure 1).
evidence: This is fundamental genetic knowledge underlying Mendelian randomization.

claim: Genetic alleles associated with physical activity, sedentary behavior, and BMI can be used to assign individuals according to higher or lower mean levels of these exposures in a randomized manner.
source: Since genotypes are randomly allocated at conception, genetic alleles associated with physical activity, sedentary behavior, and body mass index (BMI) can be used to assign individuals according to higher or lower mean levels of these exposures in a randomized manner (Figure 1).
evidence: This is the principle of Mendelian randomization, established methodological knowledge.

claim: The study used accelerometer-based physical activity and sedentary time data for 91,105 adults.
source: Here, we aimed to assess the causality between the genetic liability of physical inactivity, sedentary time and BMI by applying bidirectional Mendelian randomization analyses on summary results of accelerometer-based physical activity and sedentary time for 91,105 adults and of BMI for 806,834 adults.
evidence: This describes the data used in the study.

claim: The study used BMI data for 806,834 adults.
source: Here, we aimed to assess the causality between the genetic liability of physical inactivity, sedentary time and BMI by applying bidirectional Mendelian randomization analyses on summary results of accelerometer-based physical activity and sedentary time for 91,105 adults and of BMI for 806,834 adults.
evidence: This describes the data used in the study.

claim: Higher vigorous physical activity is causal for lower BMI with a beta of -0.16 (95% CI: -0.24, -0.08) and p = 3.8 × 10-4.
source: We found evidence of causality between higher vigorous and moderate physical activity and lower BMI (p = 3.8 × 10–4 and p = 0.006, respectively)
evidence: This is a primary finding from the CAUSE Mendelian randomization analysis presented in the Results section and Table 1.

claim: Higher moderate physical activity is causal for lower BMI with a beta of -0.18 (95% CI: -0.3, -0.05) and p = 0.006.
source: We found evidence of causality between higher vigorous and moderate physical activity and lower BMI (p = 3.8 × 10–4 and p = 0.006, respectively)
evidence: This is a primary finding from the CAUSE Mendelian randomization analysis presented in the Results section and Table 1.

claim: More sedentary time is causal for higher BMI with a beta of 0.11 (95% CI: 0.02, 0.20) and p = 0.02.
source: We found evidence of causality between higher vigorous and moderate physical activity and lower BMI (p = 3.8 × 10–4 and p = 0.006, respectively), and between more sedentary time and higher BMI (p = 0.02) (Table 1, Figure 2, and Appendix 1—table 1 and Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This is a primary finding from the CAUSE Mendelian randomization analysis presented in the Results section, Table 1, and Figure 2.

claim: Each one hour daily increase in moderate physical activity causally decreased BMI by approximately 0.27 kg/m2 (~0.8 kg).
source: In absolute units, we approximate that each one hour daily increase in moderate physical activity or decrease in sedentary time causally decreased BMI by 0.27 kg/m2 (~0.8 kg) or 0.14 kg/m2 (~0.4 kg) (Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: This is a conversion of the causal effect to absolute units based on the study's data analysis.

claim: Each one hour daily decrease in sedentary time causally decreased BMI by approximately 0.14 kg/m2 (~0.4 kg).
source: In absolute units, we approximate that each one hour daily increase in moderate physical activity or decrease in sedentary time causally decreased BMI by 0.27 kg/m2 (~0.8 kg) or 0.14 kg/m2 (~0.4 kg) (Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: This is a conversion of the causal effect to absolute units based on the study's data analysis.

claim: The median shared effect ranged from -0.01 to 0 for all trait pairs, indicating no bias induced by horizontal pleiotropy.
source: The median shared effect, which reflects the effect induced by correlated horizontal pleiotropy, ranged from –0.01 to 0 for all trait pairs, indicating that there was no bias induced by horizontal pleiotropy.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the CAUSE analysis results regarding pleiotropy.

claim: The low q values under the causal model (q = 0.18–0.20) suggested that horizontal pleiotropy was limited.
source: The low q values under the causal model (q = 0.18–0.20), which reflect the proportion of variants that show correlated horizontal pleiotropy, also suggested that horizontal pleiotropy was limited.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the CAUSE analysis q values from the study's results.

claim: No evidence of outlier variants was found in the causal association between BMI and sedentary time.
source: We checked for the existence of possible outlier variants that could have a large effect on the exposure but no effect on the outcome, by producing a scatter plot for CAUSE test statistics on the causal association between BMI and sedentary time (Appendix 1—figure 1). While CAUSE is not sensitive to outliers as such, the existence of outlier variants could provide evidence against the causal model. However, we found no evidence of outlier variants.
evidence: This is based on visual inspection of scatter plots from the analysis.

claim: The genetic correlation between BMI and sedentary time is modest (rg=0.27).
source: However, the genetic correlation analysis suggested only a modest genetic correlation between BMI and sedentary time (rg=0.27), which provides further reassurance that our CAUSE results are valid.
evidence: This is a result from genetic correlation analysis performed in the study.

claim: There is no evidence of a causal effect of BMI on vigorous physical activity (p = 0.35).
source: In the reverse direction, we found no evidence of a causal effect of BMI on vigorous physical activity (p = 0.35) or moderate physical activity (p = 0.31) using CAUSE (Table 1, Figure 2, and Appendix 1—table 1 and Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the CAUSE Mendelian randomization analysis in the reverse direction.

claim: There is no evidence of a causal effect of BMI on moderate physical activity (p = 0.31).
source: In the reverse direction, we found no evidence of a causal effect of BMI on vigorous physical activity (p = 0.35) or moderate physical activity (p = 0.31) using CAUSE (Table 1, Figure 2, and Appendix 1—table 1 and Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the CAUSE Mendelian randomization analysis in the reverse direction.

claim: There is evidence of a causal effect of BMI on more sedentary time (p = 6.3 × 10-4).
source: However, we found evidence of a causal effect of BMI on more sedentary time (p = 6.3 × 10–4), indicating bidirectional causality between the traits.
evidence: This is a finding from the CAUSE Mendelian randomization analysis showing reverse causality.

claim: There is bidirectional causality between sedentary time and BMI.
source: However, we found evidence of a causal effect of BMI on more sedentary time (p = 6.3 × 10–4), indicating bidirectional causality between the traits.
evidence: This is inferred from finding significant causal effects in both directions between sedentary time and BMI.

claim: Each kg/m2 (~3 kg) increase in BMI is causally associated with a 3.5 min increase in sedentary time per day.
source: In absolute units, we approximate that each kg/m2 (~3 kg) increase in BMI was causally associated with a 3.5 min increase in sedentary time per day (Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: This is a conversion of the causal effect to absolute units based on the study's data analysis.

claim: The median shared effect in the causal association between BMI and sedentary time was zero.
source: The median shared effect in the causal association between BMI and sedentary time was zero and the q value was 0.18, suggesting that the causal association between sedentary time and BMI was unlikely to be biased by horizontal pleiotropy.
evidence: This is a result from the CAUSE analysis indicating lack of pleiotropy bias.

claim: The q value for the causal association between BMI and sedentary time was 0.18.
source: The median shared effect in the causal association between BMI and sedentary time was zero and the q value was 0.18, suggesting that the causal association between sedentary time and BMI was unlikely to be biased by horizontal pleiotropy.
evidence: This is a result from the CAUSE analysis.

claim: The causal association between sedentary time and BMI is unlikely to be biased by horizontal pleiotropy.
source: The median shared effect in the causal association between BMI and sedentary time was zero and the q value was 0.18, suggesting that the causal association between sedentary time and BMI was unlikely to be biased by horizontal pleiotropy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the median shared effect and q value results.

claim: A less stringent threshold of p < 5 × 10-7 was used to identify genetic instruments for vigorous physical activity, moderate physical activity and sedentary time.
source: Due to the low number of independent, genome-wide significant loci for vigorous physical activity, moderate physical activity and sedentary time that were present in the GWAS results for BMI, we used a less stringent threshold of p < 5 × 10–7 to identify genetic instruments for these traits, resulting in 5, 3, and 5 independent loci, respectively.
evidence: This describes a methodological decision made in the study.

claim: Using the less stringent threshold resulted in 5 independent loci for vigorous physical activity.
source: Due to the low number of independent, genome-wide significant loci for vigorous physical activity, moderate physical activity and sedentary time that were present in the GWAS results for BMI, we used a less stringent threshold of p < 5 × 10–7 to identify genetic instruments for these traits, resulting in 5, 3, and 5 independent loci, respectively.
evidence: This is a result of applying the less stringent threshold in the analysis.

claim: Using the less stringent threshold resulted in 3 independent loci for moderate physical activity.
source: Due to the low number of independent, genome-wide significant loci for vigorous physical activity, moderate physical activity and sedentary time that were present in the GWAS results for BMI, we used a less stringent threshold of p < 5 × 10–7 to identify genetic instruments for these traits, resulting in 5, 3, and 5 independent loci, respectively.
evidence: This is a result of applying the less stringent threshold in the analysis.

claim: Using the less stringent threshold resulted in 5 independent loci for sedentary time.
source: Due to the low number of independent, genome-wide significant loci for vigorous physical activity, moderate physical activity and sedentary time that were present in the GWAS results for BMI, we used a less stringent threshold of p < 5 × 10–7 to identify genetic instruments for these traits, resulting in 5, 3, and 5 independent loci, respectively.
evidence: This is a result of applying the less stringent threshold in the analysis.

claim: The directions of causal estimates from IVW, Egger, weighted median and weighted mode methods were consistent with the findings from CAUSE, but the evidence for causality was weaker.
source: The directions of causal estimates were consistent with the findings from CAUSE, but the evidence for causality was weaker (Table 2, Figure 2, Appendix 1, and Appendix 1—table 4).
evidence: This is a comparison of results from different Mendelian randomization methods.

claim: Higher vigorous physical activity is causal for lower body fat percentage (p = 1.4 × 10-6).
source: The results from CAUSE analyses for BFP were consistent with those for BMI, that is there was evidence of a causal effect of higher vigorous and moderate physical activity on lower BFP (p = 1.4 × 10–6 and p = 0.004, respectively)
evidence: This is a finding from CAUSE analysis using body fat percentage as the outcome.

claim: Higher moderate physical activity is causal for lower body fat percentage (p = 0.004).
source: The results from CAUSE analyses for BFP were consistent with those for BMI, that is there was evidence of a causal effect of higher vigorous and moderate physical activity on lower BFP (p = 1.4 × 10–6 and p = 0.004, respectively)
evidence: This is a finding from CAUSE analysis using body fat percentage as the outcome.

claim: More sedentary time is causal for higher body fat percentage (p = 0.009).
source: The results from CAUSE analyses for BFP were consistent with those for BMI, that is there was evidence of a causal effect of higher vigorous and moderate physical activity on lower BFP (p = 1.4 × 10–6 and p = 0.004, respectively), and a causal effect of more sedentary time on higher BFP (p = 0.009) (Figure 2, Appendix 1—table 6 and Appendix 1—table 7, Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from CAUSE analysis using body fat percentage as the outcome.

claim: There is no evidence of a causal relationship between physical activity or sedentary time and waist circumference adjusted for BMI.
source: We found no evidence of a causal relationship between physical activity or sedentary time and measures of central adiposity, including WCadjBMI and WHRadjBMI (Figure 2, Appendix 1—table 6 and Appendix 1—table 7, Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from CAUSE analysis using central adiposity measures as outcomes.

claim: There is no evidence of a causal relationship between physical activity or sedentary time and waist-hip ratio adjusted for BMI.
source: We found no evidence of a causal relationship between physical activity or sedentary time and measures of central adiposity, including WCadjBMI and WHRadjBMI (Figure 2, Appendix 1—table 6 and Appendix 1—table 7, Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from CAUSE analysis using central adiposity measures as outcomes.

claim: The bidirectional causal relationship between sedentary time and BMI suggests that decreasing sedentary time is beneficial for weight management.
source: The present Mendelian randomization analyses suggest a bidirectional causal relationship between higher sedentary time and higher BMI, implying that decreasing sedentary time is beneficial for weight management, but also that reducing adiposity may lead to additional health benefits by reducing sedentary time.
evidence: This is an interpretation and implication drawn from the bidirectional causality finding.

claim: Reducing adiposity may lead to additional health benefits by reducing sedentary time.
source: The present Mendelian randomization analyses suggest a bidirectional causal relationship between higher sedentary time and higher BMI, implying that decreasing sedentary time is beneficial for weight management, but also that reducing adiposity may lead to additional health benefits by reducing sedentary time.
evidence: This is an interpretation and implication drawn from the bidirectional causality finding.

claim: There is a causal association between higher levels of physical activity and lower BMI.
source: The analyses also suggest there is a causal association between higher levels of physical activity and lower BMI, supporting the view that preventive programs for increasing physical activity and decreasing sedentary time are beneficial for weight management.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding regarding physical activity and BMI.

claim: Preventive programs for increasing physical activity and decreasing sedentary time are beneficial for weight management.
source: The analyses also suggest there is a causal association between higher levels of physical activity and lower BMI, supporting the view that preventive programs for increasing physical activity and decreasing sedentary time are beneficial for weight management.
evidence: This is an implication drawn from the causal findings of the study.

claim: A previous observational study found a bidirectional relationship where higher sedentary time at baseline increased 10-year weight gain and higher baseline weight was associated with unfavorable 10-year change in sedentary time.
source: Our results are well in accordance with a previous observational study that aimed to assess the bidirectional relationship between physical activity and weight change during a 10-year period (Barone Gibbs et al., 2020). Examining associations between accelerometer-based activity measures and weight change in 866 men and women, the study suggested a bidirectional relationship where higher sedentary time at baseline increased 10-year weight gain and higher baseline weight was associated with an unfavorable 10-year change in sedentary time.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited observational study.

claim: In a previous observational study, 1 hr lower sedentary time at baseline was associated with ~0.3 kg decrease in body weight over 10 years.
source: The effect sizes indicated that 1 hr lower sedentary time at baseline was associated with ~0.3 kg decrease in body weight over the 10-year follow up, whereas 3 kg higher baseline body weight was associated with ~2 min increase in sedentary time, closely resembling the causal estimates we observed in the present Mendelian randomization analyses.
evidence: This is a summary of effect sizes from a cited observational study.

claim: In a previous observational study, 3 kg higher baseline body weight was associated with ~2 min increase in sedentary time.
source: The effect sizes indicated that 1 hr lower sedentary time at baseline was associated with ~0.3 kg decrease in body weight over the 10-year follow up, whereas 3 kg higher baseline body weight was associated with ~2 min increase in sedentary time, closely resembling the causal estimates we observed in the present Mendelian randomization analyses.
evidence: This is a summary of effect sizes from a cited observational study.

claim: The results are in accordance with randomized clinical trials of physical activity interventions which generally suggest that increasing physical activity leads to moderate loss of body weight in overweight or obese participants.
source: Our results are also in accordance with randomized clinical trials of physical activity interventions which generally suggest that increasing physical activity leads to a moderate loss of body weight in overweight or obese participants (Church et al., 2009; Rosenkilde et al., 2012; Golubic et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2019; Biddle et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison with findings from cited randomized clinical trials.

claim: Meta-analyses of randomized clinical trials have suggested weight losses ranging from 0.3 kg to 1.8 kg for various physical activity interventions ranging from 2 to 52 weeks.
source: Resembling the causal estimates we observed, meta-analyses of randomized clinical trials have suggested weight losses ranging from 0.3 kg to 1.8 kg for various physical activity interventions ranging from 2 to 52 weeks (Twells et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited meta-analysis.

claim: Causal estimates from Mendelian randomization represent lifelong effects rather than effects lasting a defined length of an intervention.
source: However, it is important to note that the causal estimates from Mendelian randomization are not fully comparable to those from randomized clinical trials, because they represent lifelong effects rather than effects lasting a defined length of an intervention, and furthermore, physical activity interventions may operate on body weight through other pathways than those affected by the genotypes.
evidence: This is established methodological knowledge about the interpretation of Mendelian randomization results.

claim: Physical activity interventions may operate on body weight through other pathways than those affected by the genotypes.
source: However, it is important to note that the causal estimates from Mendelian randomization are not fully comparable to those from randomized clinical trials, because they represent lifelong effects rather than effects lasting a defined length of an intervention, and furthermore, physical activity interventions may operate on body weight through other pathways than those affected by the genotypes.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration about the interpretation of Mendelian randomization results.

claim: The causal effect of higher adiposity on sedentary time has not been assessed in randomized clinical trials to date, likely due to ethical and practical limitations.
source: The causal effect of higher adiposity on sedentary time has not been to date assessed in randomized clinical trials, likely due to the ethical and practical limitations of performing such a study.
evidence: This is a statement about the absence of certain types of studies with speculation about the reasons.

claim: A previous Mendelian randomization analysis found evidence for a causal, bidirectional relationship between overall activity levels and higher BMI using the maximum likelihood method.
source: In a previous Mendelian randomization analysis of adult populations, evidence for a causal, bidirectional relationship between overall activity levels and higher BMI was observed using the maximum likelihood method, but the results showed evidence of horizontal pleiotropy that could not be fully accounted for and the role of activity intensity level remained unclear (Doherty et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited Mendelian randomization study.

claim: A previous Mendelian randomization analysis showed evidence of horizontal pleiotropy that could not be fully accounted for.
source: In a previous Mendelian randomization analysis of adult populations, evidence for a causal, bidirectional relationship between overall activity levels and higher BMI was observed using the maximum likelihood method, but the results showed evidence of horizontal pleiotropy that could not be fully accounted for and the role of activity intensity level remained unclear (Doherty et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a summary of limitations from a cited Mendelian randomization study.

claim: A one-sample Mendelian randomization study in 4296 children at 11 years of age from the United Kingdom indicated a causal association between higher BMI and lower accelerometer-based moderate and moderate-to-vigorous physical activity and more sedentary time.
source: The first study, including 4296 children at 11 years of age from the United Kingdom, indicated a causal association between higher BMI and lower accelerometer-based moderate and moderate-to-vigorous physical activity and more sedentary time (Richmond et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited Mendelian randomization study in children.

claim: A one-sample Mendelian randomization study in 679 children at age 3-8 years from Denmark indicated that higher BMI is causal for higher accelerometer-based sedentary time, but did not find causality for moderate or moderate-to-vigorous physical activity.
source: The second study, including 679 children at age 3–8 years from Denmark, also indicated that higher BMI is causal for higher accelerometer-based sedentary time, but did not find a causality for moderate or moderate-to-vigorous physical activity (Schnurr et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited Mendelian randomization study in children.

claim: The differences between studies could be due to different applied methods, methodological limitations such as weak instrument bias when smaller sample sizes are used, or differences between children and adults in physical activity patterns.
source: The differences between studies could be due to different applied methods, or methodological limitations, such as weak instrument bias when smaller sample sizes are used, which may lead to estimated causal effects towards the observational association. One could also expect differences between children and adults given the distinct patterns by which they engage in physical activity.
evidence: This is speculation about reasons for differences between studies.

claim: Physical activity in adults consists of commuting, occupational and structured leisure-time activities, while children primarily engage in spontaneous, play-oriented activities.
source: For example, while physical activity in adults consists of commuting, occupational and structured leisure-time activities, children primarily engage in spontaneous, play-oriented activities.
evidence: This is established knowledge about differences in physical activity patterns between adults and children.

claim: Higher BMI leads to higher perceived exertion during physical activity.
source: Higher BMI leads to higher perceived exertion during physical activity (Groslambert and Mahon, 2006), which could reduce the natural inclination of children to engage in play-oriented activities, whereas adults exert more conscious control over their daily activities.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Groslambert and Mahon, 2006.

claim: Higher perceived exertion during physical activity could reduce the natural inclination of children to engage in play-oriented activities.
source: Higher BMI leads to higher perceived exertion during physical activity (Groslambert and Mahon, 2006), which could reduce the natural inclination of children to engage in play-oriented activities, whereas adults exert more conscious control over their daily activities.
evidence: This is speculation about how perceived exertion might affect children's physical activity.

claim: Adults exert more conscious control over their daily activities compared to children.
source: Higher BMI leads to higher perceived exertion during physical activity (Groslambert and Mahon, 2006), which could reduce the natural inclination of children to engage in play-oriented activities, whereas adults exert more conscious control over their daily activities.
evidence: This is general knowledge about behavioral differences between adults and children.

claim: The study used genome-wide summary results for objectively measured physical activity and sedentary time.
source: The strengths of the present studies include the use of genome-wide summary results for objectively measured physical activity and sedentary time, which avoided misreporting bias evident for self-reported measures
evidence: This describes a methodological strength of the study.

claim: Objectively measured physical activity and sedentary time avoid misreporting bias evident for self-reported measures.
source: The strengths of the present studies include the use of genome-wide summary results for objectively measured physical activity and sedentary time, which avoided misreporting bias evident for self-reported measures
evidence: This is established methodological knowledge about the advantages of objective measures.

claim: The study used a newly developed Mendelian randomization method that utilizes full genome-wide summary results to improve statistical power, correct for sample overlap, and assess horizontal pleiotropy.
source: as well as the use of newly developed Mendelian randomization method that utilizes full genome-wide summary results to improve statistical power, correct for sample overlap, and assess horizontal pleiotropy, successfully applied in recent Mendelian randomization studies (Jäger et al., 2020; Mitchell et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes a methodological strength of the study with supporting citations.

claim: Other sources of bias in the measurement of physical activity and sedentary time cannot be excluded, including the observer effect and the limited 7-day period of measurement.
source: The limitations are that we cannot exclude other sources of bias in the measurement of physical activity and sedentary time that could influence the observed causal estimates, including the observer effect and the limited 7-day period of the measurement, which may not be representative of long-term activity habits.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: The 7-day measurement period may not be representative of long-term activity habits.
source: The limitations are that we cannot exclude other sources of bias in the measurement of physical activity and sedentary time that could influence the observed causal estimates, including the observer effect and the limited 7-day period of the measurement, which may not be representative of long-term activity habits.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Statistical power was limited because very few genome-wide significant loci have been identified for objectively measured physical activity.
source: Furthermore, even if we used the largest available data on objectively measured physical activity, the statistical power was limited, as very few genome-wide significant loci have thus far been identified.
evidence: This is a limitation based on the current state of genetic research.

claim: The results should be replicated when larger sample sizes for accelerometer-based physical activity become available.
source: When larger sample sizes for accelerometer-based physical activity become available, the results should be replicated.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claim: The findings are not generalizable across different age-groups or populations.
source: The present study is also limited in the fact that the findings are not generalizable across different age-groups or populations.
evidence: This is a limitation acknowledged by the authors.

claim: Further research is needed to investigate causal relationships at various BMI thresholds.
source: Moreover, further research is needed to investigate causal relationships at various BMI thresholds.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research.

claim: Lifelong preventive programs for increasing physical activity and decreasing sedentary time are beneficial for weight management.
source: Our analyses also suggest that there is a causal association between higher levels of physical activity and lower BMI, supporting the view that lifelong preventive programs for increasing physical activity and decreasing sedentary time are beneficial for weight management.
evidence: This is an implication drawn from the causal findings of the study.

claim: The physical activity GWAS included up to 91,105 individuals from the UK Biobank.
source: The physical activity GWAS included up to 91,105 individuals for accelerometer-based vigorous physical activity, moderate physical activity, or sedentary time from the UK Biobank (Klimentidis et al., 2018; Doherty et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the data source used in the study.

claim: In the UK Biobank study, accelerometer was worn continuously for at least 72 hr and up to 7 days.
source: In these studies, accelerometer was worn continuously for at least 72 hr and up to 7 days.
evidence: This describes the measurement protocol in the source data.

claim: Vigorous physical activity was defined as the fraction of accelerations > 425 milli-gravities.
source: Vigorous physical activity was defined as the fraction of accelerations > 425 milli-gravities, and moderate physical activity was predicted using a machine-learning method for moderate intensity activity time (Doherty et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the operational definition used in the source data.

claim: Moderate physical activity was predicted using a machine-learning method for moderate intensity activity time.
source: Vigorous physical activity was defined as the fraction of accelerations > 425 milli-gravities, and moderate physical activity was predicted using a machine-learning method for moderate intensity activity time (Doherty et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the operational definition used in the source data.

claim: Sedentary time was defined as the time spent in activities with metabolic equivalent of task (MET) ≤1.5 during sitting, lying, or in reclining posture, except for driving and certain non-desk work instances where MET ≤2.5 was applied.
source: Sedentary time was defined as the time spent in activities with metabolic equivalent of task (MET) ≤1.5 during sitting, lying, or in reclining posture, except for driving and certain non-desk work instances where MET ≤2.5 was applied (Doherty et al., 2018).
evidence: This describes the operational definition used in the source data.

claim: For BMI, the study utilized GWAS results from a meta-analysis of the GIANT Consortium and the UK Biobank data, including altogether 806,834 individuals of European ancestry.
source: For BMI, we utilized GWAS results from a meta-analysis of the Genetic Investigation of Anthropometric Traits (GIANT Consortium) and the UK Biobank data, including altogether 806,834 individuals of European ancestry (Pulit et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the data source used in the study.

claim: For IVW, weighted median, weighted mode, and MR-Egger regression methods, only the GIANT Consortium BMI meta-analysis data of 339,224 individuals without the UK Biobank data was used to avoid sample overlap.
source: For Mendelian randomization analyses using the inverse variance-weighted (IVW), weighted median, weighted mode, and MR-Egger regression methods, we used only the GIANT Consortium BMI meta-analysis data of 339,224 individuals without the UK Biobank data to avoid sample overlap between the exposure and outcome traits as these methods are sensitive to bias from overlapping samples (Locke et al., 2015).
evidence: This describes a methodological decision to avoid bias from sample overlap.

claim: IVW, weighted median, weighted mode, and MR-Egger regression methods are sensitive to bias from overlapping samples.
source: For Mendelian randomization analyses using the inverse variance-weighted (IVW), weighted median, weighted mode, and MR-Egger regression methods, we used only the GIANT Consortium BMI meta-analysis data of 339,224 individuals without the UK Biobank data to avoid sample overlap between the exposure and outcome traits as these methods are sensitive to bias from overlapping samples (Locke et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established methodological knowledge about these Mendelian randomization methods.

claim: GWAS results for body fat percentage were available from an analysis of 454,633 participants of European ancestry in the UK Biobank.
source: GWAS results for BFP were available from an analysis of 454,633 participants of European ancestry in the UK Biobank (Elsworth et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the data source used in the study.

claim: GWAS results for waist circumference adjusted for BMI were available from GIANT Consortium meta-analyses of 231,355 individuals of European ancestry.
source: GWAS results for WCadjBMI and WHRadjBMI were available from GIANT Consortium meta-analyses of 231,355 and 694,649 individuals of European ancestry, respectively (Justice et al., 2017; Pulit et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the data source used in the study.

claim: GWAS results for waist-hip ratio adjusted for BMI were available from GIANT Consortium meta-analyses of 694,649 individuals of European ancestry.
